behavior_items: The reproducer builds a tiny metaprogramming pipeline around a non-type template parameter of placeholder type `auto`. `make_bool_metafunction<Fn>` takes a compile-time value `Fn` and exposes a nested class template `fn<Ts...>` whose `value` is always `true`. The actual body of `fn` is unimportant; what matters is that the enclosing class template depends on an `auto` NTTP and that a nested template is later named through that specialization.

`mp_copy_if<L, P>` is a stand-in for a real type-list algorithm. It takes a type `L` and a template-template parameter `P`, then simply aliases `type = L`. Because it ignores `P`, the test isolates parsing/lookup/instantiation behavior: the compiler only needs to accept `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn` as a valid template argument, not actually instantiate filtering logic.

`copy_if<TypeList, Predicate>` is the key alias: `typename mp_copy_if<TypeList, make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn>::type`. This exercises dependent-name lookup for a nested class template inside a class template specialization whose argument is an `auto` NTTP. The `template` disambiguator is required because `fn` is a dependent template member of `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>`.

Inside `test3`, the second template argument to `copy_if` is an unnamed templated lambda: `[]<typename T>() { return true; }`. A lambda expression in this position becomes a constant expression designating a unique closure object, so it is valid as an `auto` non-type template argument in modern C++. The lambda itself has a templated call operator, but `make_bool_metafunction` never invokes it; the reproducer only relies on the lambda being accepted as a structural NTTP value.

The templated lambda being passed directly as the `Predicate` argument is what makes this case special. Simpler cases with ordinary function pointers, non-generic lambdas, or lambdas not combined with a nested member template can compile, because they do not force GCC down the same instantiation/lookup path. This reproducer specifically combines: an `auto` NTTP, a lambda literal used directly as that NTTP, and later naming a nested template from the resulting specialization.

`using l1 = copy_if<mp_list<>, ...>;` should resolve to `mp_list<>`, because `mp_copy_if` always returns its first parameter unchanged. The following `return is_same_v<l1, l1>;` is just a forced use of the alias so the compiler must instantiate the alias chain and cannot discard it as unused. Since `is_same_v` is hardcoded to `true`, any failure is necessarily due to template handling before semantic evaluation of the boolean.

At instantiation time, GCC incorrectly diagnoses `no class template named 'fn' in 'struct make_bool_metafunction<<lambda> >'`. That means GCC successfully forms the specialization `make_bool_metafunction<lambda-object>` far enough to print it in diagnostics, but then loses or fails to find the nested member template `fn` during dependent lookup or substitution. The nested template is present in the primary definition, so the error indicates a compiler bug rather than invalid source.

The bug report notes the failure is a regression on GCC 14/15/16 and bisects to commit `d025b6880cde2cb2063b4d34546cdd70e5526e74` (and corresponding GCC 15 commit `f04dc89a991ddc6c08ac92c8ad29c6915c4ecafa`). That strongly suggests a front-end change in template processing caused specializations of class templates with lambda NTTPs to mishandle member template visibility or canonicalization.

Semantically, the program is well-formed: the lambda is a valid NTTP argument, `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>` is a valid specialization, `fn` is a declared nested class template, and the alias should instantiate cleanly. Therefore the reproducer exercises a wrong-rejection bug in GCC's C++ front end, not undefined behavior, not template argument mismatch, and not a missing `template` or `typename` keyword issue.

The minimal structure of the reproducer is deliberate. Every helper (`is_same_v`, `mp_list`, `mp_copy_if`) is reduced to the simplest form that still forces the compiler to perform the problematic operation. That makes the failure attributable specifically to the interaction between templated lambdas as `auto` NTTPs and lookup of an inner template member used as a template-template argument.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer is a minimized C++ template-metaprogramming test that should compile by passing a templated lambda as an `auto` non-type template argument, specializing `make_bool_metafunction` with it, and then naming the specialization's nested class template `fn` as a template-template argument. `mp_copy_if` ignores that argument and simply returns the original list type, so the only real requirement is that GCC correctly recognize `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn`. Instead, affected GCC 14/15/16 builds wrongly reject the code with `no class template named 'fn'`, showing a regression in front-end handling of member-template lookup/instantiation for class template specializations whose `auto` NTTP is a lambda closure object, especially a templated lambda.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a wrong-rejection in GCC C++ front-end template handling, not a problem in the source program. The code is intentionally minimized so that almost nothing semantic happens except: (1) form a class template specialization `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>` where `Predicate` is an `auto` NTTP bound to a direct lambda expression, specifically a templated lambda closure object; and then (2) name the specialization's nested member class template `::template fn` as a template-template argument. Because `mp_copy_if` ignores that template argument and simply aliases its first parameter, the failure must occur before any meaningful metafunction logic, during substitution, dependent lookup, or specialization formation. The diagnostic proves GCC can form `make_bool_metafunction<<lambda>>` well enough to print it, but then incorrectly loses visibility of the nested template `fn` that is unconditionally declared in the primary template. The strongest pattern is therefore an internal mismatch in how GCC represents or canonicalizes class template specializations whose `auto` NTTP is a lambda closure object, causing member-template lookup on that specialization to fail. The fact that simpler variants reportedly compile, while this one requires the combination of lambda NTTP + nested member template + template-template argument, points to a defect in dependent-name lookup / substitution logic for member templates of specializations involving lambda NTTPs. The regression note and bisected commit further suggest a front-end change in template processing around lambda/NTTP representation, specialization comparison, or member lookup introduced the bug.
possible_causes: Incorrect dependent member-template lookup in `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn` when the enclosing specialization depends on an `auto` NTTP whose value is a lambda closure object; GCC likely fails to find nested templates on that specialization even though they exist in the primary template.

Broken canonicalization or identity/equality handling for lambda closure objects used as structural non-type template arguments, causing the specialization `make_bool_metafunction<lambda>` to be represented inconsistently between specialization creation and later member lookup.

A substitution bug in template-template argument processing for dependent nested templates, where `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn` is mishandled specifically when `Predicate` is a lambda NTTP rather than a simpler constant-expression NTTP.

Regression in class template specialization instantiation metadata for `auto` NTTPs, such that the instantiated/specialized type loses its member template list or is treated as an incomplete/alternate variant during lookup.

Faulty interaction between generic lambdas (templated call operator) and NTTP structural value processing, leading GCC to classify the lambda-based specialization differently from ordinary NTTP values and thereby break nested-template access.

A front-end bug in cp/pt logic that handles `typename`/`template` dependent qualifiers on current instantiation substitutes, incorrectly concluding that `fn` is not a class template after substitution even though parsing and source semantics are valid.
evidence: `mp_copy_if` ignores its template-template parameter and just returns `L`, so the compiler only needs to accept `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn`; no real algorithmic instantiation is involved.

`fn` is explicitly declared as a nested class template in the primary template `make_bool_metafunction<Fn>`, so `no class template named 'fn'` indicates lookup/substitution failure inside GCC rather than missing source declarations.
The error names `struct make_bool_metafunction<<lambda> >`, showing GCC successfully formed or at least recognized the specialization with the lambda NTTP before failing member-template lookup.

The reproducer uses a direct templated lambda as an `auto` NTTP and then names a nested template from the resulting specialization; this exact combination is the distinguishing trigger described in the behavior analysis.
The lambda itself is never invoked, and `is_same_v` is hardcoded `true`, eliminating runtime semantics and pointing squarely to compile-time template handling.

The bug report states this is a regression affecting GCC 14/15/16 and bisects to a specific commit, strongly supporting a compiler implementation defect introduced by a front-end change rather than invalid code.

Other similar test functions reportedly compile, implying the failure is not general rejection of lambdas or NTTPs but a narrower path involving nested member template lookup on lambda-based specializations.

The required `template` disambiguator is present in `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn`, so the rejection is not explained by missing syntax and instead suggests GCC mishandles dependent qualified-id resolution after substitution.

selected_files.reason: Most likely location: this file implements C++ template processing, substitution, dependent-name handling, and instantiation. The failure is a wrong rejection when naming `make_bool_metafunction<Predicate>::template fn`, so the bug likely lives in template-template argument handling or lookup during instantiation here.

The reproducer depends on a templated lambda used directly as an `auto` NTTP. This file builds lambda expressions and closure objects, so a regression in representing lambda closure types/values for template arguments could explain why the specialization loses `fn`.

This file handles declarations, member declarations, and class/template setup in the C++ front end. If the nested class template `fn` is being registered, attached, or later retrieved incorrectly, that logic would plausibly involve declaration processing here.

Template-related parsing and deferred semantic actions go through this file. The bug is triggered at compile-time semantic analysis, so a mistake in how dependent qualified-ids or template-template arguments are finalized could surface here.

The diagnostic says GCC cannot find the nested class template `fn` in a valid specialization. That points to member/template lookup or binding resolution, which is handled in the C++ name-lookup machinery in this file.

Template arguments, lambda closure objects, and specialization identity rely on underlying tree node canonicalization and comparison. If the lambda NTTP is represented inconsistently, lookup of the specialized class template could fail downstream.

Some generic front-end tree/type utilities used by both C and C++ live here. It is less likely than the C++-specific files, but still a possible place for shared tree handling that affects template argument formation or canonical types.

The bug is unlikely to be here, but global compiler context can influence shared caches and type identities. Include it only as a low-probability shared-state candidate if the regression stems from stale or mismatched cached tree objects.

Template/lambda NTTP handling depends on hashing and equality of tree objects in many internal maps. If the lambda closure object or specialization key is mis-hashed or mis-compared, lookup could miss the nested template even though it exists.

Lower-probability supporting candidate: several compiler internals use hash maps to store template and type metadata. A bad key identity path for lambda NTTPs could cause the specialization state to be stored or retrieved incorrectly.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: static int maybe_adjust_types_for_deduction (tree tparms, unification_kind_t strict, tree* parm, tree* arg, tree arg_expr)

ARG is the type of the argument passed to the call, or the type of the value initialized with the result of the conversion function. ARG_EXPR is the original argument expression, which may be null.

Core DR 115: In contexts where deduction is done and fails, or in contexts where deduction is not done, if a template argument list is specified and it, along with any default template arguments, identifies a single function template specialization, then the template-id is an lvalue for the function template specialization.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: static int unify (tree tparms, tree targs, tree parm, tree arg, int strict, bool explain_p)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Deduce the value of template parameters. TPARMS is the (innermost) set of template parameters to a template. TARGS is the bindings for those template parameters, as determined thus far; TARGS may include template arguments for outer levels of template parameters as well. PARM is a parameter to a template function, or a subcomponent of that parameter; ARG is the corresponding argument. This function attempts to match PARM with ARG in a manner consistent with the existing assignments in TARGS. If more values are deduced, then TARGS is updated. Returns 0 if the type deduction succeeds, 1 otherwise. The parameter STRICT is a bitwise or of the following flags: UNIFY_ALLOW_NONE: Require an exact match between PARM and ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_MORE_CV_QUAL: Allow the deduced ARG to be more cv-qualified (by qualification conversion) than ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_LESS_CV_QUAL: Allow the deduced ARG to be less cv-qualified than ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_DERIVED: Allow the deduced ARG to be a template base class of ARG, or a pointer to a template base class of the type pointed to by ARG. UNIFY_ALLOW_INTEGER: Allow any integral type to be deduced. See the TEMPLATE_PARM_INDEX case for more information. UNIFY_ALLOW_OUTE
Note that DECL can be defined in this translation unit, if required.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: int more_specialized_fn (tree pat1, tree pat2, int len)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Given two function templates PAT1 and PAT2, return: 1 if PAT1 is more specialized than PAT2 as described in [temp.func.order]. -1 if PAT2 is more specialized than PAT1. 0 if neither is more specialized. LEN indicates the number of parameters we should consider (defaulted parameters should not be considered). The 1998 std underspecified function template partial ordering, and DR214 addresses the issue. We take pairs of arguments, one from each of the templates, and deduce them against each other. One of the templates will be more specialized if all the *other* template's arguments deduce against its arguments and at least one of its arguments *does* *not* deduce against the other template's corresponding argument. Deduction is done as for class templates. The arguments used in deduction have reference and top level cv qualifiers removed. Iff both arguments were originally reference types *and* deduction succeeds in both directions, an lvalue reference wins against an rvalue reference and otherwise the template with the more cv-qualified argument wins for that pairing (if neither is more cv-qualified, they both are equal). Unlike regular deduction, after all the arguments have been d

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: static int more_specialized_partial_spec (tree tmpl, tree pat1, tree pat2)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Determine which of two partial specializations of TMPL is more specialized. PAT1 is a TREE_LIST whose TREE_VALUE is the TEMPLATE_DECL corresponding to the first partial specialization. The TREE_PURPOSE is the innermost set of template parameters for the partial specialization. PAT2 is similar, but for the second template. Return 1 if the first partial specialization is more specialized; -1 if the second is more specialized; 0 if neither is more specialized. See [temp.class.order] for information about determining which of two templates is more specialized.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: static tree get_bindings (tree fn, tree decl, tree explicit_args, bool check_rettype)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Return the template arguments that will produce the function signature DECL from the function template FN, with the explicit template arguments EXPLICIT_ARGS. If CHECK_RETTYPE is true, the return type must also match. Return NULL_TREE if no satisfactory arguments could be found.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: static tree get_partial_spec_bindings (tree tmpl, tree spec_tmpl, tree args)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Return the innermost template arguments that, when applied to a partial specialization SPEC_TMPL of TMPL, yield the ARGS. For example, suppose we have: template <class T, class U> struct S {}; template <class T> struct S<T*, int> {}; Then, suppose we want to get `S<double*, int>'. SPEC_TMPL will be the partial specialization and the ARGS will be {double*, int}. The resulting vector will be {double}, indicating that `T' is bound to `double'.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: // Compare two function templates T1 and T2 by deducing bindings // from one against the other. If both deductions succeed, compare // constraints to see which is more constrained. static int more_specialized_inst (tree t1, tree t2)

gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: TEMPLATES is a TREE_LIST. Each TREE_VALUE is a TEMPLATE_DECL. Return the TREE_LIST node with the most specialized template, if any. If there is no most specialized template, the error_mark_node is returned. Note that this function does not look at, or modify, the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of any of the nodes. Since the node returned is one of the elements of INSTANTIATIONS, callers may store information in the TREE_PURPOSE or TREE_TYPE of the nodes, and retrieve it from the value returned.

If DECL is a specialization of some template, return the most general such template. Otherwise, returns NULL_TREE. For example, given: template <class T> struct S { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int>::f(U)' this will return the full template. This function will not trace past partial specializations, however. For example, given in addition: template <class T> struct S<T*> { template <class U> void f(U); }; if TMPL is `template <class U> void S<int*>::f(U)' this will return `template <class T> template <class U> S<T*>::f(U)'.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: tree most_specialized_partial_spec (tree target, tsubst_flags_t complain, bool rechecking )
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Return the most specialized of the template partial specializations which can produce TARGET, a specialization of some class or variable template. The value returned is a TEMPLATE_INFO; the TI_TEMPLATE is a TEMPLATE_DECL node corresponding to the partial specialization, while the TI_ARGS is the set of template arguments that must be substituted into the template pattern in order to generate TARGET. The result is cached in the TI_PARTIAL_INFO of the corresponding TEMPLATE_INFO unless RECHECKING is true. If the choice of partial specialization is ambiguous, a diagnostic is issued, and the error_mark_node is returned. If there are no partial specializations matching TARGET, then NULL_TREE is returned, indicating that the primary template should be used.

gcc/cp/pt.cc.signature: static void regenerate_decl_from_template (tree decl, tree tmpl, tree args)
gcc/cp/pt.cc.summary: Given a function DECL, which is a specialization of TMPL, modify DECL to be a re-instantiation of TMPL with the same template arguments. TMPL should be the template into which tsubst'ing should occur for DECL, not the most general template. One reason for doing this is a scenario like this: template <class T> void f(const T&, int i); void g() { f(3, 7); } template <class T> void f(const T& t, const int i) { } Note that when the template is first instantiated, with instantiate_template, the resulting DECL will have no name for the first parameter, and the wrong type for the second. So, when we go to instantiate the DECL, we regenerate it.
Return the TEMPLATE_DECL into which DECL_TI_ARGS(DECL) should be substituted to get DECL.
Returns true if we need to instantiate this template instance even if we know we aren't going to emit it.
If FN has a noexcept-specifier that hasn't been instantiated yet, instantiate it now, modifying TREE_TYPE (fn). Returns false on error, true otherwise.

DECL is a FUNCTION_DECL that is a template specialization. Return its type -- but without substituting the innermost set of template arguments. So, innermost set of template parameters will appear in the type.

Returns TRUE if the EXPRESSION is type-dependent, in the sense of [temp.dep.expr]. Note that an expression with no type is considered dependent. Other parts of the compiler arrange for an expression with type-dependent subexpressions to have no type, so this function doesn't have to be fully recursive.

[temp.dep.expr]/5: A class member access expression (5.2.5) is type-dependent if the expression refers to a member of the current instantiation and the type of the referenced member is dependent, or the class member access expression refers to a member of an unknown specialization. This function returns true if the OBJECT in such a class member access expression is of an unknown specialization.
walk_tree callback function for instantiation_dependent_expression_p, below. Returns non-zero if a dependent subexpression is found.

Returns TRUE if the EXPRESSION is instantiation-dependent, in the sense defined by the ABI: "An expression is instantiation-dependent if it is type-dependent or value-dependent, or it has a subexpression that is type-dependent or value-dependent." Except don't actually check value-dependence for unevaluated expressions, because in sizeof(i) we don't care about the value of i. Checking type-dependence will in turn check value-dependence of array bounds/template arguments as needed.

Returns TRUE if LIST (a TREE_LIST whose TREE_VALUEs are expressions) contains any value-dependent expressions.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of them throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. On entry, DECL_INITIAL (decl1) should be NULL_TREE or error_mark_node, or may be a BLOCK if the function has been defined previously in this translation unit. gcc/cp/semantics.cc.summary: Helper function for handle_omp_array_sections. Called recursively to handle multiple array-section-subscripts. C is the clause, T current expression (initially OMP_CLAUSE_DECL), which is either a TREE_LIST for array-section-subscript (TREE_PURPOSE is low-bound expression if specified, TREE_VALUE length expression if specified, TREE_CHAIN is what it has been specified after, or some decl. TYPES vector is populated with array section types, MAYBE_ZERO_LEN set to true if any of the array-section-subscript could have length of zero (explicit or implicit), FIRST_NON_ONE is the index of the first array-section-subscript which is known not to have length of one. Given say: map(a[:b][2:1][:c][:2][:d][e:f][2:5]) FIRST_NON_ONE will be 3, array-section-subscript [:b], [2:1] and [:c] all are or may have length of 1, array-section-subscript [:2] is the first one known not to have length 1. For array-section-subscript <= FIRST_NON_ONE we diagnose non-contiguous arrays if low bound isn't 0 or length isn't the array domain max + 1, for > FIRST_NON_ONE we can if MAYBE_ZERO_LEN is false. MAYBE_ZERO_LEN will be true in the above case though, as some lengths could be zero.

Hidden name, either friend declaration or built-in function, are not ignored. WHERE controls which scopes are considered. It is a bit mask of LOOK_where::BLOCK (look in block scope), LOOK_where::CLASS (look in class scopes) & LOOK_where::NAMESPACE (look in namespace scopes). It is an error for no bits to be set. These scopes are searched from innermost to outermost. WANT controls what kind of entity we'd happy with. LOOK_want::NORMAL for normal lookup (implicit typedefs can be hidden). LOOK_want::TYPE for only TYPE_DECLS, LOOK_want::NAMESPACE for only NAMESPACE_DECLS. These two can be bit-ored to find namespace or type. WANT can also have LOOK_want::HIDDEN_FRIEND or LOOK_want::HIDDEN_LAMBDa added to it.

Look up NAME for type used in elaborated name specifier in the scopes given by HOW. Unlike lookup_name_1, we make sure that NAME is actually declared in the desired scope, not from inheritance, nor using directive. For using declaration, there is DR138 still waiting to be resolved. Hidden name coming from an earlier friend declaration is also returned, and will be made visible unless HOW is TAG_how::HIDDEN_FRIEND. A TYPE_DECL best matching the NAME is returned. Wrap a SAVE_EXPR around EXPR, if appropriate. Do this to any expression which may be used in more than one place, but must be evaluated only once. Normally, expand_expr would reevaluate the expression each time. Calling save_expr produces something that is evaluated and recorded the first time expand_expr is called on it. Subsequent calls to expand_expr just reuse the recorded value. The call to expand_expr that generates code that actually computes the value is the first call *at compile time*. Subsequent calls at compile time* generate code to use the saved value. This produces correct result provided that *at run time* control always flows through the insns made by the first expand_expr before reaching the other places where the save_expr was evaluated. You, the caller of save_expr, must make sure this is so. Constants, and certain read-only nodes, are returned with no SAVE_EXPR because that is safe. Expressions containing placeholders are not touched; see tree.def for an explanation of what these are used for.

Subroutine of stabilize_reference; this is called for subtrees of references. Any expression with side-effects must be put in a SAVE_EXPR to ensure that it is only evaluated once. We don't put SAVE_EXPR nodes around everything, because assigning very simple expressions to temporaries causes us to miss good opportunities for optimizations. Among other things, the opportunity to fold in the addition of a constant into an addressing mode often gets lost, e.g. "y[i+1] += x;". In general, we take the approach that we should not make an assignment unless we are forced into it - i.e., that any non-side effect operator should be allowed, and that cse should take care of coalescing multiple utterances of the same expression should that prove fruitful.

Stabilize a reference so that we can use it any number of times without causing its operands to be evaluated more than once. Returns the stabilized reference. Any other kind of expression is returned unchanged.

Return OP, stripped of any conversions to wider types as much as is safe. Converting the value back to OP's type makes a value equivalent to OP. If FOR_TYPE is nonzero, we return a value which, if converted to type FOR_TYPE, would be equivalent to converting OP to type FOR_TYPE. OP must have integer, real or enumeral type. Pointers are not allowed! There are some cases where the obvious value we could return would regenerate to OP if converted to OP's type, but would not extend like OP to wider types. If FOR_TYPE indicates such extension is contemplated, we eschew such values. For example, if OP is (unsigned short)(signed char)-1, we avoid returning (signed char)-1 if FOR_TYPE is int, even though extending that to an unsigned short would regenerate OP, since the result of extending (signed char)-1 to (int) is different from (int) OP.

gcc/c-family/c-common.cc.summary: Walk the tree X, and record accesses to variables. If X is written by the parent tree, WRITER is the parent. We store accesses in one of the two lists: PBEFORE_SP, and PNO_SP. If this expression or its only operand forces a sequence point, then everything up to the sequence point is stored in PBEFORE_SP. Everything else gets stored in PNO_SP. Once we return, we will have emitted warnings if any subexpression before such a sequence point could be undefined. On a higher level, however, the sequence point may not be relevant, and we'll merge the two lists. Example: (b++, a) + b; The call that processes the COMPOUND_EXPR will store the increment of B in PBEFORE_SP, and the use of A in PNO_SP. The higher-level call that processes the PLUS_EXPR will need to merge the two lists so that eventually, all accesses end up on the same list (and we'll warn about the unordered subexpressions b++ and b. A note on merging. If we modify the former example so that our expression becomes (b++, b) + a care must be taken not simply to add all three expressions into the final PNO_SP list. The function merge_tlist takes care of that by merging the before-SP list of the COMPOUND_EXPR into its after-SP list

The whole point here is to end up with a situation where each and every ..._TYPE node the compiler creates will be uniquely associated with AT MOST one node representing a typedef name. This way, even though the compiler substitutes corresponding ..._TYPE nodes for TYPE_DECL (i.e. "typedef name") nodes very early on, later parts of the compiler can always do the reverse translation and get back the corresponding typedef name. For example, given: typedef struct S MY_TYPE; MY_TYPE object; Later parts of the compiler might only know that `object' was of type `struct S' if it were not for code just below. With this code however, later parts of the compiler see something like: struct S' == struct S typedef struct S' MY_TYPE; struct S' object; And they can then deduce (from the node for type struct S') that the original object declaration was: MY_TYPE object; Being able to do this is important for

If we manage to add a fix-it hint, then the location of the fix-it hint is likely to be more useful as the primary location of the diagnostic than that of the following token, so we swap these locations. For example, given this bogus code: 123456789012345678901234567890 1 | int missing_semicolon (void) 2 | { 3 | return 42 4 | } we will emit: "expected ';' before '}'" RICHLOC's primary location is at the closing brace, so before "swapping" we would emit the error at line 4 column 1: 123456789012345678901234567890 3 | return 42 |< fix-it hint emitted for this line | ; | 4 | } |< "expected ';' before '}'" emitted at this line | ^ | It's more useful for the location of the diagnostic to be at the fix-it hint, so we swap the locations, so the primary location is at the fix-it hin
